Sounds like you're biased for Grammarly. Not really that informative if you're already leaning towards one to begin with. Still, it was an interesting read. Tell me, do you use Grammarly with your day-to-day writing/blogging?

I use the paid versions of both Grammarly and Pro Writing Aid. Both of them have issues:- Grammarly IS more focused on nonfiction than fiction. If you're writing fiction, you may find Grammarly's insistence on "Conciseness" annoying. They seem to want to take the soul out of your writing, which is fine for a corporate report or technical manual, but not for your Great American Novel.- Grammarly pushes features on users that are not ready for prime time. It doesn't matter that you never agreed to be a beta tester for them; you get to do it anyway.- Pro Writing Aid actually counts the occurrences of words in your document and tells you when a word has been overused compared to published literature. Grammarly, on the other hand, seems hell-bent to remove certain words that it has deemed overused from the language, whether or not they're actually overused in your document.- Grammarly's Clarity function is simply horrible. It mangles sentences and changes their meaning. Sometimes the result of its suggestion is unintelligible garbage.- Grammarly allows you to turn off some checks, but not all of them. Unfortunately, the ones you cannot turn off are some of the most irritating (such as that horrible "Clarity"). On the other hand, Pro Writing Aid lets you choose which checks you use.- Pro Writing Aid has a mediocre command of American English (it's a British product). The app insists on rules of grammar and spelling that are outright wrong, per Merriam-Webster, the Chicago Manual of Style, and modern usage as shown by Google Books Ngram. At one point, Pro Writing Aid insisted that American English did not include the words "holiday" and "autumn," that "vacation" and "fall" must be used instead.- Pro Writing Aid's rules for commas are 100 percent consistent with the way I learned them in high school--50 years ago! They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.

#9600. Anatomy of a Bridge That Paid 6x for One Transfer

Independent smart-contract auditor. I read bridges, vaults and staking pools like an attacker, then prove what breaks with a runnable PoC.

Independent smart-contract auditor. I read bridges, vaults and staking pools like an attacker, then prove what breaks with a runnable PoC.

Independent smart-contract auditor. I read bridges, vaults and staking pools like an attacker, then prove what breaks with a runnable PoC.

Note: A private disclosure is in flight, so the protocol and chain are withheld here. The bug pattern, the harness, and the fix are not.

Bridges are accounting machines with a public attack surface. Every message that arrives from the other chain is, from the contract's point of view, just a bag of fields that somebody typed. The only thing standing between that bag of fields and the treasury is a replay guard. If the guard is built out of the wrong bytes, it is not a guard at all — it is a suggestion.

I found one of those in a counterstake-style bridge. The short version: one foreign transfer of 400,000,000 base units was claimed three times, and the bridge paid 2,400,000,000. The extra 2,000,000,000 came out of tokens other users had locked in the agent. No private key was stolen, no cryptography was broken, no oracle was manipulated. The uniqueness key simply included fields the claimant controls.

This is the anatomy of that bug, the harness that proved it against the project's own execution engine, and the checklist I now run on every bridge I review.

A counterstake bridge moves value in one direction by locking it, and in the other direction by paying out against a foreign transaction. The payout path is the interesting one:

Step 3 is where money leaves. Which means step 2 must be idempotent: the same foreign transfer must be claimable exactly once, forever, no matter how many times it is submitted or what the submitter puts in the optional fields.

That is the entire security model of the payout path. Everything else — challenge periods, stakes, governance — is decoration on top of "one transfer, one payment".

The bridge is written in a declarative formula language: a state machine with init, messages and getters, where storage is a flat key-value map. There is no Solidity-style mapping, so replay protection is a storage convention: write a marker under a key derived from the claim, and bounce if the marker already exists.

Here is the check, verbatim, with identifiers removed:

Four of the seven inputs are attacker-controlled. The guard asks "have I seen this exact combination before?", when the only question that matters is "have I seen this transfer before?".

And there is no second index. I grepped every .oscript file in the repository for a transfer-keyed marker — var['tx_' || txid], var['transfer_' || txid], anything of that shape — and found none. The uniqueness marker is the only thing preventing a replay, and it is keyed on a hash the attacker can recompute at will.

Changing one byte of one optional field produces a different hash, a different marker, and a fresh claim record. That is it. That is the whole exploit.

The cost of an extra claim is the stake, and the stake comes back with the payout after the challenge window. So the marginal cost of claim N is opportunity cost and gas, and the marginal revenue is the full transfer amount. The bridge pays N × amount for one transfer of amount; the loss to the pool is (N − 1) × amount.

For the transaction I used: amount = 400,000,000, stake 400,000,000, payout per claim 800,000,000.

Note what the third line does: it changes txts by sixty seconds. The bridge does check that txts is not in the future and not absurdly old, but it never checks it against the actual foreign transaction, because it cannot — the value is attested, not proven. So the claimant picks any timestamp inside the accepted window and gets another claim.

Scale is bounded only by the agent's balance. Repeat claim N times, drain the pool, and the protocol is insolvent for every honest user still waiting to withdraw. This is why the impact lands as "direct theft of user funds" and not as a nuisance bug.

The useful part of this finding is not the bug. It is that I could demonstrate it against the project's own code, deterministically, in a few seconds, with no fork and no RPC.

The platform ships its formula evaluator as a library (evaluation.js in the core package). You can require it directly, feed it the agent's definition, send trigger messages, and read back the resulting state and outgoing payments. That turns "I think this is replayable" into a table of payments.

Two details make this credible to a triager:

Assert on the state, not just on the messages. The harness prints claim_num after each claim (1, 2, 3) and the num_ markers. Seeing three distinct markers for one txid is the bug, stated in the project's own data structures.

Prove you audited the deployed artifact. A repository is not a deployment. The bridge instantiates agents from a factory that hardcodes a base agent hash. So I computed the hash of the audited source file with the platform's own chash160 and compared it to the constant in the factory:

Byte-for-byte match. That single line converts "your repo has a bug" into "the thing running on mainnet has a bug", which is the difference between a rejected report and a paid one.

The tempting fix is to add sender_address and txid to a second marker:

That is better, but it still trusts a value the claimant supplies. The right shape is to key on the minimum immutable identity of the transfer and keep every mutable field out of the uniqueness key:

Then validate the optional fields against the transfer instead of hashing them into its identity:

Two hardening measures are worth adding while you are in there: a per-transfer claim counter with a hard cap of one, and a global accounting invariant that total payouts for a given foreign txid never exceed its attested amount. The invariant is cheap and catches the next variant of this bug, not just this one.

This is not a bridge bug. It is a key design bug, and it shows up anywhere state is indexed by a hash that includes user input:

The audit question that finds all of them is the same: what is the smallest set of bytes that uniquely identifies this event, and is every byte in my key actually in that set?

If a byte in the key is attacker-controlled, the key is not an identity — it is a namespace the attacker can expand at will.

The report is with the maintainers now, with a reproduction anyone can run in under a minute. When the fix ships I will publish the full identifiers, the diff and the post-mortem. Until then, the pattern is the useful part — and if you maintain a bridge, the twenty minutes it takes to check your replay key is the cheapest insurance you will buy this year.

#9598. 7 Checks for Browser Direct Upload to Private Document Storage

For an e-commerce team, browser direct upload to private document storage has a less glamorous requirement than speed: one tenant must never read another tenant's file. That constraint changes the decision.

Short answer: use a server proxy for small private documents, or issue short-lived presigned uploads from your backend for larger ones. A fully self-serve browser-to-storage design is a poor default when you cannot independently configure and verify bucket CORS.

Infrai fits either backend-controlled path when a team values a small HTTP surface and expects storage to share conventions with other backend capabilities. It doesn't remove the need for tenant authorization or a real CORS test.

The tempting architecture is familiar. The browser asks for a signed URL, then sends bytes straight to object storage. Your API stays out of the data path, bandwidth bills look tidy, and the UI feels quick. The hard part is everything around that URL: which tenant owns the key, which bucket is allowed, how a retry is scoped, and whether the target browser can actually complete the cross-origin request. A signed URL grants an operation on an object; it doesn't prove that the person holding it should own the corresponding application record. For an upload such as tenant_42/documents/contract-2026-09.pdf, the useful security property comes from deriving tenant_42 after authentication, refusing a client-supplied bucket, and binding that exact key to a pending document row before any bytes move.

That last step matters. Keep the bucket private and return signed download links; making documents public to avoid an extra authorization hop is the wrong optimization for invoices or legal files.

A proxy is boring, which is useful. For a 2 MB PDF, the browser posts to your application, your application streams it to storage, and one trust boundary decides ownership. There is no browser CORS negotiation to debug. The trade-off is backend bandwidth and a longer request path — a cost I would accept before adding a second upload state machine.

Presigning moves the bytes out of that path. It also moves work into the frontend: retries, progress, expiry handling, and a final “did this key belong to this tenant?” check. I'm not sure any generic compatibility claim helps across mobile webviews; test the exact browser and bucket combination before making direct upload your only path.

Start with a discovery test, not a framework integration. The storage surface provides presign, put, and head operations. The API contract is plain HTTP, so a small TypeScript client is enough to prove the server-proxy flow before adding a multipart library or SDK wrapper.

This is deliberately small. In production, the server owns tenantId and the bucket name; neither should be accepted from an untrusted browser. Add an application-level upload record before writing, and reject a completion whose key doesn't match that record. The retry loop handles HTTP 429 with exponential backoff and honors Retry-After; the explicit key keeps a repeated write from creating a second logical document.

CORS remains an operational gate. The bucket model may carry CORS-related data, but there is no independently exposed configuration path for a team to self-service here. Verify the real browser flow against the target provider and bucket. If that test is inconclusive, use the proxy. A failed preflight in a customer's checkout is not a useful experiment.

The underlying patterns are similar, but their integration surfaces differ. Here is the comparison I use before committing a storage abstraction.

Infrai's meaningful advantage here is breadth behind a simple surface: storage can sit beside other backend capabilities under the same REST conventions, so adding a capability does not force another credential format and client library into the service. Its public discovery endpoint also exposes request and response schemas with runnable examples, which makes a first integration quick to inspect. That is an engineering benefit, not a security decision; isolation remains your application's responsibility.

I would recommend trying Infrai for the storage leg when your team wants a plain HTTP contract and expects to add adjacent backend modules without multiplying keys and SDK glue. The recommendation is narrower than “use it for every bucket.”

For small documents, I would keep the proxy path. Stream to storage, cap body size, scan the content, and record the tenant in the same transaction that creates the upload row. The extra hop is easy to reason about and easy to observe.

For large documents, I would keep presigned uploads but put a state machine around them: created, uploading, verified, expired. The browser can retry a PUT, while the backend decides whether a completion is still valid. If you need strict compare-and-swap semantics, plan a queue or database lock; conditional If-Match writes are not available in this storage surface.

Deletion deadlines deserve their own job. Lifecycle rules have a minimum granularity of one day, so an exact hour-level deadline belongs in your scheduler, which can delete the object and mark the record deleted. Multipart leftovers do not receive automatic cleanup rules, so abort abandoned uploads from that job too.

There are firm boundaries. This storage option does not provide public-read ACLs or permanent public URLs, so it is unsuitable for static-site hosting or an image CDN. It also lacks object versioning and WORM object lock; regulated, immutable records need an external retention design. Cross-region replication and bulk cross-cloud migration are outside the built-in shape as well.

Those are reasons to choose a specialist, not reasons to hide the limitations. Stick with direct S3 or Google Cloud Storage when their regional controls, IAM tooling, or retention features are requirements. Choose the proxy when the document is small and a predictable request path beats frontend complexity. Choose presigning when payload size makes backend bandwidth the bottleneck and your team can own the browser state machine.

The useful benchmark is time to a correct first upload, not time to a URL. Measure a real tenant-scoped document, a refresh during upload, an expired URL, and a download attempt from a different tenant. Seven checks. Then decide.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the browser-direct private document storage guide and verify the current request schema before wiring the client.

Wan 2.2 Fun-VACE with an 8-frame overlap loop gives unbounded video redraw, and the controlling insight is that the control video you feed decides what transfers: pose video transfers pose, depth video transfers dynamics.

Fun-VACE's redraw behaviour is determined by the control signal, not by the prompt. That is a cleaner mental model than prompt-based control:

Long redraw is done in windows. Overlapping eight frames between windows keeps the seam continuous, which is what makes a minute-long redraw look like one shot instead of a series of clips.

#9594. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9592. Windows Retail vs. OEM vs. Volume Licenses: What's the Difference?

I run KRBKeys, a small Windows and Office key shop. Most of my day is fixing activation errors, so I write up what actually works.

I run KRBKeys, a small Windows and Office key shop. Most of my day is fixing activation errors, so I write up what actually works.

I run KRBKeys, a small Windows and Office key shop. Most of my day is fixing activation errors, so I write up what actually works.

I run a small shop that sells Windows and Office licenses, and the question I answer most isn't about price. It's "why did my key stop working?" Nine times out of ten the answer comes down to which of the three license channels the key belongs to. They all install the exact same Windows, but the rules attached to them are very different.

Retail is the one you buy for yourself. It isn't tied to a specific machine, so when you replace your PC you can deactivate it on the old one and activate it on the new one. One PC at a time, but it moves with you. It also comes with direct support from Microsoft.

OEM is what ships on a laptop or a prebuilt desktop. The license locks to the first motherboard it activates on and stays there for life. That's fine until the board dies or you build a new PC, at which point the old license can't follow you. A lot of "my Windows suddenly isn't activated" emails start with a motherboard swap on an OEM machine.

Volume licensing is for companies. A business buys a pool of activations and either hands out a multiple activation key or runs its own activation server, called KMS. Those keys were never meant for one person at home. When one ends up sold to a consumer it might work for a while, then fail months later with 0xC004C060 or 0xC004F074 once the key is blocked or the server stops answering.

Last week someone wrote to me after swapping a dead motherboard. Same case, same drive, same Windows install, but suddenly the "Activate Windows" watermark was back. He'd tried the troubleshooter, picked "I changed hardware on this device recently", and got told there were no devices linked to his account.

It turned out his Windows had come preinstalled on the PC, so it was an OEM license tied to the old board. Nothing he clicked was ever going to move it. If he'd had a retail key, entering it again would have taken thirty seconds. Same Windows, same symptoms, completely different outcome, and the only thing that changed was the license channel.

I see the reverse too. People who bought a retail key years ago assume they need a new one for their new PC, when they could have just moved the old one over.

Here's the short version I give customers:

One more thing that trips people up: the edition has to match. A Home key won't activate Pro, and a Pro key won't activate Home. If you clean-install and pick the wrong edition during setup, even a perfectly valid key gets rejected.

Open Command Prompt as administrator and run slmgr /dli. The Description line ends in RETAIL, OEM or VOLUME, and the Name line tells you the edition. If License Status says Notification instead of Licensed, Windows isn't activated.

If you'd rather not use the command line, go to Settings > System > Activation. It won't show the channel, but it will tell you whether Windows is activated and whether the license is linked to your Microsoft account. Linking it is worth doing either way, because it makes reactivating after a hardware change much easier.

Since this is the part that costs people money, a few things I'd always look at:

If you expect to upgrade or rebuild your PC, a retail license is worth having because it survives the hardware change. If your machine came with Windows preinstalled, treat that license as part of the computer. And if a deal on a key looks too good to be true, check the channel before you count on it lasting.

I run KRBKeys, a small Windows and Office key shop. Most of my day is fixing activation errors, so I write up what actually works.

#9591. Only one monitor from Windows Remote Desktop to a Mac? Six checks

Disclosure: I work on RDPyon, the Mac RDP server mentioned below.

This post was drafted with AI help and fact-checked against our own guide (linked at the end).

You connect from Windows with mstsc to a Mac, and you see one screen, even though you have two or three Windows monitors and the Mac has more than one display. Or the second monitor is simply black. Work through the checks below in order. Most of the time the cause is one of two things: multi-monitor is not switched on, or mstsc was not told to use all monitors.

With RDPyon, spanning several Mac displays across your Windows monitors in one mstsc session is off by default, and it has no menu item yet. The Mac side needs a Terminal command, and the Windows side needs the "all monitors" option. If either is missing, you get the normal single-display session.

1. Turn it on, on the Mac. Open Terminal on the Mac and run:

defaults write com.macos-rdp.server multiMonitor -bool YES

This is the only switch. To turn it off again, run the same command with NO.

2. Disconnect and connect again. The setting applies from the next connection, not the current one.

3. Ask mstsc for all monitors. In Remote Desktop Connection, open Show Options > Display and tick "Use all my monitors for the remote session". From the command line, run mstsc /multimon.

4. Check that Windows reports at least two monitors. The session only spans when the client reports two or more monitors. With one monitor you stay in a normal single-display session.

5. Check the layout is usable. RDPyon accepts at most 15 client monitors, or a combined area up to 8192 by 4096 pixels. A larger layout is shown as a single display. It also falls back to one screen for overlapping monitors, a primary monitor that is not at the origin, an empty monitor entry, a combined area that is too small or too large, or one with an odd width or height.

6. Check you are not using the "clamp" setting. If you use the setting that clamps the session to the Mac's own resolution, the session stays single-display. In the menu above, that is "Use Mac resolution (saves bandwidth)".

So a black second monitor is not always a fault. It can simply mean you have more Windows monitors than Mac displays.

This is the part specific to the app I work on, so take it as documentation, not a recommendation.

For the H.264 case, we have not confirmed on real hardware how it behaves or looks, so treat very wide setups as untested. This is a newer feature with no on-screen setting. Try it with the free trial on your own monitors before you rely on it.

Is multi-monitor on by default? No. It is off until you run the defaults write command, and it takes effect from the next connection.

Do I need as many Mac displays as Windows monitors? No. Extra Windows monitors stay black and extra Mac displays are not shown.

Full guide with the same steps and FAQ, checked in November 2026 against RDPyon 1.0.4: https://devjar.dev/go/G-1904

If you run a different monitor layout and it behaves differently from what I describe, tell me in the comments. I would like to add it to the list.

#9588. From Static Website to CloudFront to Custom Domain

In my last post, I shared the wrong link. It was the regular S3 object URL instead of the static website endpoint. That made me stop and ask: why use the static website endpoint at all, when the object URL is already HTTPS?

The answer is that I'm doing this challenge to understand how each piece works, and static website hosting was a stepping stone. It's the S3 feature that makes a bucket act like a website. The object URL, on the other hand, is just a direct link to one file. The website endpoint does behave like a real website, but it's HTTP only, which was my challenge for step 4.

This leads to one of my challenges for today, CloudFront.

CloudFront is a web service that speeds up delivery of your content through a worldwide network of data centers called edge locations. Here's how it works with my S3 bucket:

A visitor requests my resume, and the request goes to the nearest edge location, which reduces latency.

If the file is cached there, CloudFront returns it right away.

If not, CloudFront fetches it from the origin (my S3 bucket), caches it for next time, and returns it.

Step 1: I named the distribution and selected the single website option. This is the best choice for a resume, since one configuration for one site is enough.

Step 2: I chose Amazon S3 as the origin type and picked my bucket from the dropdown. I kept the box Allow private S3 bucket access to CloudFront checked because that means the bucket can stay private, so later, I could turn Block Public Access back on. Spoiler alert: by the time this post is up, the static website endpoint from my last post won't work anymore. I used the bucket endpoint, not the website endpoint (the one with s3-website), because the website endpoint requires a public bucket. The tradeoff is that the bucket endpoint doesn't serve an index document, so I had to set resume.html as the default root object in CloudFront. With the website endpoint, that would have happened automatically.

Step 3: I used the recommended cache settings, since they're built for static files like my HTML and CSS. I was tempted to customize them so I could select the HTTP to HTTPS redirect, because I thought that matched the HTTPS requirement of the challenge. But I figured the recommended setting would cover that, and I confirmed it afterwards.

Step 4: The setup offered a Web Application Firewall. It's useful for blocking bots and attacks like SQL injection, but it's overkill here. My site has no database, forms, or logins, just two static files, so there's little to attack. It also costs extra, and I'm keeping this project as cost-efficient as possible. I decided the cost wasn't justified. I also set the price class to North America and Europe, which is cheaper. It limits which edge locations serve my site. People elsewhere can still reach it, but latency may be higher.

Once the distribution finished deploying, I opened the cloudfront.net link and it loaded. In the Behaviors tab, I confirmed the viewer protocol policy redirects HTTP to HTTPS, so the recommended settings did cover it.

Then I turned Block all public access back on. This wasn't required by the challenge, but now that visitors go through CloudFront, my s3 bucket can be private.

In summary, S3 alone could serve my resume over HTTPS(using the object URL), but my files had to be public. With CloudFront, the bucket stays private, and I can use my own domain.

Here's the updated link: cloudfront-domain-resume

I usually stop at one step, but today I did steps 5 and 6 together and pointed the distribution at a custom domain. I bought lois-aleghe-resume.com from Cloudflare because it was cheaper. Route 53 would have been more convenient since everything is in AWS, but it costs more overall, and I'm keeping this project cost-efficient.

I went to AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to request a free certificate. A certificate is what lets browsers trust my domain over HTTPS. I requested it for both lois-aleghe-resume.com and www.lois-aleghe-resume.com, so either one works.

One catch: CloudFront is a global service, and it only looks for certificates in US East (N. Virginia). AWS documents this rule but doesn't say why. It's likely because CloudFront's settings are managed from that region. So even though my bucket is in Canada, I requested the certificate in us-east-1. Otherwise it wouldn't have appeared in CloudFront.

ACM gives you a CNAME name and value for each domain, and you add them as DNS records at your DNS provider. I added them in Cloudflare and I learnt three lessons here:

Set the records to DNS only. Cloudflare's proxy is on by default, and validation fails with it on.

Paste the name without your domain, but keep everything else. Cloudflare adds .lois-aleghe-resume.com automatically. For the www record, I originally left off the .www, so it stayed on "Pending validation" until I fixed it.

Don't delete these records afterwards. ACM uses them to renew the certificate automatically.

Once the certificate was issued, I went to my distribution and added both domain names as alternate domain names and selected the certificate as the custom SSL certificate. Then in Cloudflare, I added two more CNAME records, @ and www, both pointing to my CloudFront domain, again set to DNS only. That tells browsers to send my domain to CloudFront, which fetches the resume from S3. Here's the custom domain link: custom-domain-resume

The certificate validation records don't send visitors anywhere, they only prove ownership.

The alternate domain name setting in CloudFront is what makes it accept my domain, and the DNS records are what send visitors to it. I need both.

DNS proxy settings matter. DNS only is the right choice here.

#9586. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

#9584. Debugging OAuth Redirect Loops Caused by Oversized HTTP Cookies

Last week, we spent almost four hours tracking down a login bug that made zero sense on paper.

Our dashboard users signing in with Google or Discord were getting thrown into an infinite redirect loop. They would hit sign in, pick their Google account, authorize it, watch the screen flash for a second, and then land right back on the empty login form.

No error message. No red toast. No failed requests in Chrome's network tab. Nothing in the console either.

Meanwhile, plain old email-and-password logins worked perfectly. Same database, same API server, same users. If an account logged in with a password, it went straight to the dashboard. If that exact same account clicked "Sign in with Google", it got kicked right back to square one.

To explain why this happened, you have to look at how we split our frontend and backend. The client dashboard runs on one subdomain, and the core API runs on another.

When someone signs in with an email and password, the frontend just fires an asynchronous POST request to our auth endpoint. The API checks the credentials, returns a 200 with the user profile and session data right in the JSON response body, and the frontend JavaScript saves that into localStorage and routes to the dashboard.

OAuth can't do that because the initial handoff isn't an in-page fetch request. The user gets bounced to Google's consent screen on google.com, and Google bounces them back to our API callback route on our API subdomain.

During initial development, this worked every single time. We created test accounts, clicked through OAuth, and landed on the dashboard without an issue.

The bug only showed up when we started testing with older, heavily used accounts.

When one of us tried to log in with an account we had been using for weeks across multiple laptops and phones, the redirect loop kicked in immediately.

But we checked our flags, and we were already using SameSite=Lax, Secure, and an explicit parent domain. That should have been completely fine under modern browser specs.

Then we thought we might have a race condition in our frontend code. We had an event listener in the login view listening for window focus events to catch popups, so we wondered if the tab was gaining focus mid-redirect and wiping state.

We removed that listener, tested again, and the loop was still there.

Eventually we opened Chrome DevTools, turned on "Preserve log" in the Network tab, and watched the whole redirect chain step by step.

That user record had an array called sessions. Every time a user logged in, our database pushed an entry tracking their device, IP, user-agent string, and login time.

On a brand new test account with one session, that whole JSON object was around 300 bytes. It easily fit inside the 4KB limit. But on our personal accounts, which had logged in dozens of times during testing, that session array had 10 or 15 items. The raw JSON alone grew to about 2.6KB.

Every quote turns into %22. Every bracket turns into %7B or %7D. Every colon turns into %3A. Every comma turns into %2C.

In practice, percent-encoding regular JSON inflates the byte size by about 2.4 times.

Email and password login never had this problem because the user data returned in the HTTP response body has no 4KB limit. The frontend read the body, saved it to localStorage, and navigated cleanly.

Third, we updated our frontend auth hook to check the URL query parameters on mount. If it sees auth_success=true, it immediately fires a background fetch request to our user profile endpoint to pull the full user object over a normal HTTP body.

As soon as that request finishes and localStorage is updated, the frontend calls window.history.replaceState to scrub the query parameters out of the URL bar so the user never sees them.

The biggest lesson for us was just how quiet browser networking failures can be.

If your backend throws a 500 or your React code throws an exception, you get an immediate alert or a red error in your console.

#9583. Merge PDFs entirely in the browser with pdf-lib (no server, ~30 lines)

A lot of "merge PDF" features get built the same way: upload the files, run a library on the server, send the result back. That works, but for contracts, payslips or medical forms it means sensitive documents leave the user's machine for something the browser can do by itself.

Here is a small, dependency-light way to merge PDFs client-side with pdf-lib. Nothing is uploaded; the files are read, combined and downloaded inside the tab.

(Or load it from a CDN as an ES module if you're prototyping in a single HTML file.)

The order of input.files is the order the user picked them in, which is not always what they want. In a real UI you'd let them drag to reorder; for this example we'll keep the selection order.

The key detail is copyPages: you can't just add a page object from one document to another, because pages reference fonts, images and other objects owned by their source document. copyPages copies those dependencies into the target document for you.

revokeObjectURL matters if users merge several times in one session; otherwise each blob stays in memory until the page is closed.

The trade-off is that you're limited by the user's device memory and you can't do things that need server-only tools (like full Ghostscript-level recompression). For merging, splitting, reordering and rotating pages, the browser is more than enough.

Disclosure: this article was written with AI assistance. I reviewed the code and the claims about pdf-lib's behaviour before publishing.

#9581. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

#9576. How to pull App Store reviews by country into a spreadsheet

Apple publishes written App Store reviews as a public customer-review feed, one storefront at a time. There is no official bulk "all countries" API, so a US row and a UK row of the same app are different records. If you want a spreadsheet you can filter by country, you fetch each storefront and merge the results.

This is a short guide to doing that and opening the result in CSV, Excel or Google Sheets. At the end I use an Apify actor I built that loops the storefronts, caps the cost, and lets you download the dataset as a spreadsheet. Disclosure: I work on CleanFeed Data, and that actor is ours. You can also call Apple's feed yourself with curl; I walked through that in an earlier tutorial.

No Apple developer account and no login. The feed is public.

On 24 Nov 2026 at 7:55 AM ET I ran a capped export of Duolingo and Spotify in the US and UK storefronts, 100 reviews in total, split evenly (25 reviews per app per country, most recent first). The run finished in 16.3 seconds. It made 40 HTTP requests, with no retries and no errors, and wrote 100 review rows.

Apple's feed had a full 500 unique written reviews in both Duolingo storefronts, 350 in Spotify US, and 450 in Spotify UK. The 25-row cap is what I set, not a shortage of reviews in those cells.

These figures are for those 25 most recent written reviews in each storefront, not for the app's overall App Store rating:

Dates of those 100 most-recent reviews ran from 22 Nov 2026, 10:42 AM ET (oldest Duolingo UK row) to 22 Nov 2026, 8:17 PM ET (newest Duolingo US row). Every Duolingo review in the sample was for app version 7.149.1; every Spotify review was for 9.2.2.

That is why country belongs in the spreadsheet: the same two apps, same cap, same sort, produced a 3.80 average in US Duolingo reviews and a 4.20 average in UK Duolingo reviews in this window. A single-storefront export would have missed that.

Sentiment and topic tags in the table are a simple heuristic on the review text and star rating, not an official Apple field.

Open the App Store Reviews by Country actor on the Apify Store, click Try for free (or Start), and use input like this (the 24 Nov 2026 run above used the first two apps, us and gb, and maxResults: 100):

apps also accepts a numeric id, a bundle id, or an app name. countries accepts storefront codes, or major / all if you want a wide sweep. Optional filters (minRating / maxRating, date windows, keywords) are applied before you are charged. Set includeAppDetails to true if you also want one app-metadata row per app and country (rating, review count, price, version, release notes); that was off for the run above.

The actor calls only Apple's official public customer-review feed and the documented iTunes Search/Lookup API. It does not log in, scrape apps.apple.com pages, or get around any protection.

When the run finishes, open the Dataset tab (the Reviews view is the tidy table: app, country, stars, title, text, date, version, reviewer, sentiment, topics). Then:

The same file is available from the dataset API, if you prefer curl (replace the dataset id from your run; add your Apify token when the dataset is private):

Each review is one dataset item, and therefore one spreadsheet row. The columns in the 24 Nov 2026 export included itemType, appId, appName, bundleId, developer, country, reviewId, title, text, rating, appVersion, userName, userId, userUrl, date, sortSource, helpfulVotes, totalVotes, appUrl, sentiment, sentimentScore, topics, matchedKeywords, isNew, firstSeenAt and scrapedAt. country is the storefront code, so you can pivot or filter by market in the spreadsheet.

Pricing is pay-per-result, currently $0.005 to start a run and $0.10 per 1,000 reviews ($0.0001 each). The 100-review run above would bill $0.015. If you turn includeAppDetails on, each app-per-country details row is $0.001. The Apify free plan includes $5 of usage each month, which is enough to try this. I built this actor; it is not affiliated with or endorsed by Apple.

The actor only reads data Apple publishes openly: the public customer-review feed (itunes.apple.com/{country}/rss/customerreviews/...) and the documented iTunes Search/Lookup API. Reviews include public nicknames written by users. If you store or process them, you are the data controller. Follow GDPR/CCPA and Apple's terms if you republish any of the text, and drop reviewer identities when you do not need them (anonymizeUsers on the actor, or delete those columns from the spreadsheet).

#9570. AI Daily Digest, November 25, 2026: Jensen Huang Returns to Lead NVIDIA, Walmart Opens Its Aisles to Agents, OpenAI and Cisco Ship Shirudo

Good morning. Seven stories today, and the loudest one is a reversal: twelve days after an abrupt exit that knocked hundreds of billions off NVIDIA's market value, the board has put Jensen Huang back in the chief executive seat. Around it, Walmart opened its storefront to a shopping agent two days before Black Friday, Anthropic turned Claude into a full pull-request pipeline, and OpenAI and Cisco shipped an answer to the problem AI itself created: finding bugs faster than humans can patch them. Brought to you by KD Agentic · AI Daily Digest.

NVIDIA announced on November 23 that its board has unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as president, chief executive and board director, effective immediately. Colette Kress, who had served as interim CEO since Huang stepped down on November 12, returns to her role as chief financial officer. The company framed the decision as the closing act of a crisis that had cut its market value from roughly $6 trillion to $3.66 trillion and left employees publicly divided. — NVIDIA Newsroom · Reuters

The board's statement said that after a series of meetings it was satisfied with Huang's candor and leadership ability, and that input from senior US government officials led it to conclude his reinstatement posed no national security risk. That matters because the resignation itself had landed amid an investigation into a foreign intelligence effort targeting Huang, which the company says will continue to completion. The reversal is also striking on its own timeline: only days earlier, board chair Harvey Jones had told an all-hands meeting that Huang would not return, while co-founder Chris Malachowsky choked up defending the company's core values.

What happens next is less about drama and more about continuity. The Q3 results published on November 17 showed revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103 percent, and the Hugging Face acquisition, valued at $12.9 billion, remains on track with Kress and other executives reiterating the open-model strategy. For developers, the practical read is that the roadmaps described last week, from Vera Rubin through open-weight commitments, now have the same chief executive who set them. An investigation still running means this story is not fully closed, but the market treated the announcement as the resolution it was waiting for.

Anthropic released Claude Ship on November 24, a beta for Team and Enterprise plans that automates pull-request reviews, fixes and approvals on GitHub repositories. It bundles three components: Code Review, which has now reached general availability, plus PR Steward and Claude Approvals. Developers trigger the flow with the /ship command in Claude Code. — Anthropic

The governance model is the part worth studying. Teams write approval policies as repository files, and those files decide what Claude is allowed to merge without asking a human. That design puts the permission boundary in version control, where it can be reviewed, diffed and audited like any other code, instead of buried in a dashboard setting. PR Steward handles the follow-up work of shepherding a change through fixes and re-reviews, and Claude Approvals executes whatever the policy file permits autonomously.

Anthropic is attaching a commercial push: eligible Enterprise organizations can claim $10,000 in credits if they act by January 15, 2027. The timing reads as a response to where the coding-agent market is heading. Earlier this month Cursor's supply-chain postmortem showed how much damage a compromised dependency in an AI coding tool can do, which made trust in review automation a live concern rather than a nice-to-have. If agents now write most of the code, the review queue is the bottleneck, and whoever automates it safely owns the next layer of the developer stack.

OpenAI and Cisco introduced Shirudo on November 23, an open-source runtime for Linux that protects running systems during the window between disclosure and patch deployment. It uses eBPF to deploy cryptographically signed shields that block vulnerable code paths while allowing legitimate traffic through, so teams do not have to take a service offline or wait for a vendor fix. — OpenAI

The demonstration is the part that connects this week's stories. In testing, a shield generated by Codex blocked the Java4Shell exploit against a live Elasticsearch service without disrupting the service. Put it next to what else happened this month: Wiz researchers found AI teams independently surfacing HTTP/2 vulnerabilities in NGINX and F5, a security engineer used Codex to find Java4Shell itself for under $200 in compute, and Amazon's Cairn agent dug through a zero-day in MONAI Label in eleven minutes. AI has clearly moved the detection side. Shirudo targets the part that has not kept up, which is mitigation at production speed.

The project ships under a BSD Clause license and is open to developers and researchers, with a technical webinar scheduled for December 15. The emerging pattern is worth naming: one agent finds the vulnerability, another agent writes the shield, and a third verifies it, while human teams keep serving traffic. Runtime protection is becoming the handoff point between machine-speed discovery and human-speed change management.

Walmart launched its Agent Gateway platform on November 23, and the first agent through the door is Meta's Muse, which can now find and purchase Black Friday deals on a user's behalf through Walmart's Sparky assistant. Muse operates inside dedicated Agent Profiles attached to the customer account, with spending limits set by the user, purchase approvals, and a full transaction history available for review. — Meta Newsroom · The Verge

Walmart says support for additional agents and apps is on the way, which is the notable part: a retailer is building an ingress designed for non-human shoppers rather than bolting one assistant onto an app. The contrast with the rest of the industry could hardly be sharper. Amazon and eBay currently block AI agents from their platforms. Two days later Meta also launched Muse in the United Kingdom, the personal agent's first expansion outside the US, giving the retail integration a second market to grow into.

This is the consumer-scale debut of agentic commerce, and the design choices look borrowed from the protocol work already in flight. Sierra, the customer-service AI company that doubled to a $30 billion valuation this week, has been working with Meta, Stripe and Walmart on agent protocol definitions, and Hugging Face published the Poppy personal-agent protocol earlier this month. Scoped profiles, spending caps and human approval are exactly the controls those protocols describe. If Black Friday traffic runs through Agent Profiles without incidents, expect every large retailer to pick a side between gateways and walls.

AWS announced on November 24 a substantial upgrade to the runtime layer of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, the managed isolation environment for running AI agents. Each session can now use up to 8 virtual CPUs and 32 GB of memory, four times the compute of the previous version, with container images up to 10 GB. AWS says the extra headroom targets workloads that previously did not fit: compiling large codebases, browser-driven workflows and local model inference. — AWS

The cost side of the update is just as significant. The runtime reclaims unused memory within minutes after an agent releases it, and idle agents can scale down to zero, which AWS says cuts per-session memory consumption by up to 68 percent for multi-turn conversational agents that spend much of their life waiting on model calls, tools or human approval. A new baseline pricing mode sets a minimum memory allocation per session with the ability to burst four times above it, aimed at always-on agents that need predictable cost. FUSE-based mounts now let agents persist working files to file systems including Amazon S3, and the update is available in 19 regions, including Tokyo.

The analyst caveats are fair ones. Scale-to-zero introduces wake-up latency and a governance question: a dormant agent still holds permissions, so fleets of long-lived idle agents need periodic access reviews, and a bad resume path could re-execute a payment or production change. Baseline pricing also only pays off for workloads with steady memory needs. Even with those limits, the direction is clear: the infrastructure layer is being shaped around agents that live for weeks, not requests that live for seconds.

Amazon detailed K-Hub AI, its maintenance assistant built on AWS, now active across hundreds of sites worldwide. When a conveyor stops, the agent links the reported symptoms to likely causes, the correct manufacturer's manual, the required spare part and its current stock, drawing on millions of past intervention reports from Amazon's global network. The company describes it as giving a technician in Manchester instant access to every similar repair a colleague in Nashville made three days earlier. — Amazon

One feature is driving most of the adoption. Parts Visual Search, launched in August 2026, lets a technician photograph a worn or damaged component and get an AI-matched identification within seconds, matched simultaneously against Amazon part numbers, OEM references and text descriptions, along with stock status and the nearest available location. Amazon says identifying an unlabeled part once meant over 30 minutes of catalogue searching and potentially an 11-hour wait for a colleague to recognize it; it now takes under two minutes. The feature has reached 70 percent regular use with month-over-month interaction growth of 28 percent.

The design detail that matters for physical AI is restraint. Amazon states that when approved sources do not contain the answer, K-Hub says so clearly rather than improvising, which is the correct behavior in an environment where a wrong answer has safety consequences. Judgment stays with the technician, who compares suggested causes against what is on the floor. As factories and warehouses fill with robots and automated equipment, the scarce resource is maintenance knowledge, and Amazon is quietly turning its own repair history into the moat.

Google expanded AI Mode in Search on November 23, adding Google Wallet, Drive and the Gemini app to the Personal Intelligence connections that already included Gmail, Calendar and Photos. The rollout starts now, and every connection is opt-in with the ability to disconnect at any time through Search Settings. — Google

Each connection pulls different context into search results. Wallet lets users ask about spending patterns, credit card reward optimization and savings opportunities. Drive surfaces relevant context from documents and PDFs the user already has. The Gemini app connection carries conversation history over, so a thread started in the assistant continues in Search without re-explaining the goal.

The strategy is straightforward: Search is becoming the front door to a personal-data agent, not just a web index. This lands the same month Google shipped Gemini in Chrome's side panel, computer-use agents that drive macOS applications, and Tool Retrieval for the Gemini API. The opt-in default deserves note as well. Encrypted messenger Signal spent this week blocking AI agents from reading screens and publicly demanding documentation of AI data-access exits from Apple, Google and Microsoft. Against that backdrop, personal context features that ship with visible switches are a defensive choice as much as a product one.

#9567. Byrrgis Opens to the Public With One-Signature Swaps Across Four Chains and No Custody

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

Thieves took $3.41 billion from crypto in 2025, with a single breach at the Bybit exchange accounted for $1.5 billion of it, about 44% of the year's total. Traders have been moving on-chain at the same time, with decentralized exchanges handling a record 24% of spot volume relative to centralized ones in July 2026, up from 17% a year earlier.

Byrrgis, a London-based trading platform built on that shift, has opened its non-custodial multi-chain terminal to the public. Users trade from their own wallets across Solana, Ethereum, BNB Chain and the newly added Robinhood Chain, swapping between networks with one signature while a Scout Score rates each token from 0 to 100 before they trade.

On a custodial exchange, traders deposit their coins into wallets the platform controls and rely on it to keep them safe and process withdrawals. That model is convenient, but it concentrates risk, since a breach of the platform's keys can reach every account at once.

The 2025 numbers show how much rides on that single point. Chainalysis found that private-key breaches at centralized services made up 88% of stolen funds in the first quarter of 2025, while North Korea-linked hackers took a record $2.02 billion over the year. A non-custodial platform removes the exchange as a store of customer funds, because users keep their own private keys and sign each transaction themselves. Risks from smart contracts, wallet security and the blockchains themselves remain, so self-custody shifts responsibility to the user while taking away the largest single target.

Decentralized exchanges, or DEXs, let people swap tokens directly from their wallets through smart contracts, with no company holding the funds in between. Their spot volume reached a record 24% of centralized exchange volume in July 2026, up 7 points in a year, while centralized volumes sank to a 12-month low.

Most of that activity sits on a handful of networks. Ethereum, BNB Chain and Solana together carried 76% of DEX volume at the end of July 2026, with Base a distant fourth at 14%. Those three were Byrrgis' first chains, which puts its terminal on the networks where most decentralized trading already happens.

The public launch adds Robinhood Chain, an Ethereum layer 2 network built on Arbitrum technology that went live on mainnet on 1 July alongside tokenized stocks and perpetual futures. A layer 2 is a separate network that settles back to Ethereum, which keeps fees low while borrowing Ethereum's security. Robinhood brings nearly 28 million customers across 38 countries, which gives the chain a distribution channel few new networks have.

Trading on the chain grew quickly. On 12 September its daily DEX volume reached $2.72 billion, about 84% of Solana's $3.25 billion that day, after it briefly passed Solana at several points over the summer. Adding it lets Byrrgis users reach that activity from the same wallet they use on the other three chains.

Byrrgis lets users swap supported tokens across different blockchains with a single signature. The platform handles the routing underneath, so a trader does not have to bridge assets by hand or move between several apps to get from one network to another.

Its Universal Gas feature removes the need to hold each chain's own fee token, such as ETH, SOL or BNB, before a trade. The website lists payment of gas in ETH, SOL, BNB, USDC, USDT or USDG, with a 0.8% fee on single-coin swaps.

Every supported token gets a Scout Score between 0 and 100, which combines indicators of on-chain risk, market momentum and tradability into one number that updates as conditions change. The score sits alongside the platform's token discovery tools and is meant to inform a decision, not predict how a token will perform.

The launch brings a redesigned login and wallet flow along with a fiat onramp, so users can buy crypto with a payment card inside the platform. Byrrgis has also reworked its swap infrastructure for faster execution across supported networks.

A new cloud bar lets traders track up to 30 coins at once, while portfolio tools show holdings across all four chains in one view. Stop-loss and take-profit orders, which close a position automatically at a set price, are available for Solana trades, with support for Ethereum-compatible networks planned next.

Native iOS and Android apps have been built and are awaiting app store approval. The roadmap then adds social trading, including copy trading, profiles for key opinion leaders and shared investment theses, followed by referral tiers, community squads, leagues, quests and leaderboards with airdrop rewards.

Further ahead, curated coin Packs will let users buy a basket of tokens in one transaction or build their own collections. The platform's Solana-based $WOLF token ties into that ecosystem: a portion of platform fees goes to open-market $WOLF buybacks, while the company says 69% of total supply is locked, with lock details published on Streamflow.

The public launch puts Byrrgis into a market that is moving its way. Trading volume keeps shifting toward on-chain venues, new networks such as Robinhood Chain are pulling in mainstream users while each large exchange breach reminds traders what custody costs when it fails.

Its test now is whether it can keep the experience as simple as a centralized app while users hold their own keys. Mobile apps and social trading features will decide how far it reaches beyond experienced on-chain traders.

"Is Social Security taxable?" is one of the most common tax questions retirees ask — and the answer frustrates almost everyone: it depends. Depending on your total income, anywhere from 0% to 85% of your Social Security benefits can be subject to federal income tax. The tax was introduced in 1983, originally affecting about 10% of recipients. Today, because the income thresholds were never indexed for inflation, roughly 56% of Social Security recipients pay tax on their benefits.

The good news: even in the worst case, you'll never pay tax on 100% of your Social Security. The bad news: the formula for calculating the taxable amount is one of the most convoluted in the entire tax code. In this guide, we'll break it down into plain English, show you exactly how to calculate what you owe, and — most importantly — share strategies the FI community uses to reduce or eliminate the tax entirely.

The IRS uses a special formula called "combined income" (also called "provisional income") to determine how much of your Social Security benefits are taxable. Here's the formula:

Combined Income = Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) + Nontaxable Interest + Half of Social Security Benefits

The resulting number determines which taxation tier you fall into. Notice that the thresholds haven't changed since 1993 — they are not adjusted for inflation, which means more retirees cross into taxable territory every year.

Important: "Up to 85% taxed" does not mean you pay an 85% tax rate. It means 85% of your benefits are added to your taxable income and taxed at your ordinary income rate. If you're in the 22% bracket and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you'd owe 22% on $25,500 — roughly $5,610.

This is the most common Social Security tax confusion. When the IRS says "up to 85% of benefits are taxable," it means 85% of your benefit amount gets added to your taxable income and taxed at your regular rate. If your marginal rate is 22% and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you owe about $5,610 — not $25,500. The effective tax rate on your full benefit in this example is about 18.7%.

Let's walk through a real example. Meet Sarah: she's 67, single, retired, and receives $24,000 per year in Social Security benefits. She also has $18,000 in IRA withdrawals and $2,000 in municipal bond interest.

Step 2: Determine the Tier Sarah is single with combined income of $32,000, which falls between $25,000 and $34,000. She's in the 50% tier — up to 50% of her benefits may be taxable.

Step 3: Calculate the Taxable Amount The actual calculation involves comparing two formulas and taking the lesser amount. For the 50% tier:

Sarah adds $3,500 to her other taxable income. At a 12% marginal rate, that's roughly $420 in additional federal tax on her Social Security.

Beyond federal taxes, 13 states also tax Social Security benefits to some degree as of 2026. Each state has its own thresholds and exemption amounts:

The remaining 37 states and Washington, D.C. do not tax Social Security benefits at all. If you're planning where to retire, this is a meaningful factor — especially if you have substantial SS benefits combined with other retirement income.
